prompt:
Write a technical description of about 800 words of how Git stores a commit, covering blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The reader is a developer who uses Git every day and has never looked inside the .git directory.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
When you run git commit, the result is stored in a small, simple database that lives inside the hidden .git directory, in a subfolder called objects. This database is a key-value store. Each entry is called an object, and its key is a SHA-1 hash (newer repositories can use SHA-256) of the object's contents. The first two hex characters of the hash become a directory name and the remaining characters become the file name, so an object with a hash starting ab12 is stored at .git/objects/ab/12 followed by the rest of the hash. Because the key is derived from the content, identical content always produces the same key, and changing a single byte produces a completely different one. Every object is compressed with zlib and, once written, is never modified. There are only four kinds of object, and three of them are what make up a commit.

The first kind is the blob, which holds the raw contents of a single file and nothing else. A blob has no file name, no permissions and no path, so it knows nothing about where it lives in your project. Two files with identical contents, even in different directories, share a single blob. Likewise, a file you edit and then revert to its earlier state points back at the blob that already exists. This is why Git can keep a long history of a large project without using much more space than the files themselves.

Since blobs carry no names, something else has to say which blob belongs at which path, and that job belongs to the tree. A tree object represents one directory. It is a list of entries, and each entry records a file mode, a name and the hash of what that name refers to. The mode tells Git whether the entry is a regular file, an executable file, a symbolic link or a subdirectory. If the entry is a file, the hash points to a blob, and if it is a subdirectory, the hash points to another tree. A whole project snapshot is therefore a tree of trees, with a single root tree at the top whose hash effectively identifies the complete state of every file in the repository at that moment. Because each tree's hash depends on the hashes of everything beneath it, changing one deeply nested file produces new hashes for its blob, for each tree above it, and for the root, while every untouched subtree is reused as it was.

The commit object is what turns a snapshot into a point in history. It is a short piece of text containing the hash of the root tree, the hash of each parent commit, the author and committer with their timestamps, and finally your commit message. An ordinary commit has one parent, the first commit in a repository has none, and a merge commit has two or more. Those parent hashes are what link commits into a chain, and because each commit's hash covers its parent's hash, the history cannot be altered without changing every commit that follows. This is also why rewriting history with a rebase gives you new commits with new hashes rather than modifying the old ones. A commit does not store a diff, either. The differences you see in git show or git log -p are computed on demand by comparing the trees of a commit and its parent.

The fourth kind of object is the annotated tag, which wraps a pointer to another object together with a name and a message. It is not part of an ordinary commit, but it is worth knowing about because it works the same way as the others.

All of these objects are identified by long hashes that nobody wants to type or remember, so Git also maintains refs, which are human-readable names for particular hashes. A ref is just a small text file containing a single commit hash. Your branches live under .git/refs/heads, so the file .git/refs/heads/main contains the hash of the latest commit on main. Tags live under .git/refs/tags, and the branches your repository has fetched from remotes live under .git/refs/remotes. When you make a new commit, Git writes the new objects, sets the new commit's parent to the commit your branch currently points at, and then updates the branch file to contain the new commit's hash. That update is the entire meaning of a branch advancing. Creating a branch is just as cheap, since it means writing a forty-character file, which is why branching in Git feels instantaneous.

One more file ties this together, called HEAD, found at .git/HEAD. Normally it does not contain a hash directly but a line such as ref: refs/heads/main, meaning that your current branch is main and that new commits should move that ref forward. If you check out a specific commit instead of a branch, HEAD holds a raw commit hash, which is what Git calls a detached HEAD. Over time Git may also pack many loose objects into a single packfile for efficiency, and may gather refs into a packed-refs file, but these are storage optimizations that do not change the model.

Putting it all together, a commit is a chain of references. HEAD names a branch, the branch file names a commit, the commit names a root tree and its parents, each tree names its subtrees and blobs, and the blobs hold your actual file contents. If you want to see this for yourself, git cat-file -p followed by a hash will print any object in readable form, and you can follow the chain from HEAD down to a single line of a single file.
